guidance.title: Hip Fracture
guidance.summary:
**All hip fractures require admission for operative management.**

**Surgical Timing:**
- Target: surgery within 24-48 hours of admission
- Each 12-hour delay beyond 48 hours increases 30-day mortality
- Delays beyond 48 hours associated with increased rates of pneumonia, pressure ulcers, DVT, and UTI
- Acceptable reasons for brief delay: active MI/ACS, acute decompensated heart failure, reversible coagulopathy requiring correction, acute pulmonary process

**Operative Approach by Fracture Type:**
- Femoral neck (nondisplaced, Garden I-II): cannulated screw fixation (in younger patients); may consider nonoperative with close follow-up in extremely high surgical risk patients
- Femoral neck (displaced, Garden III-IV): hemiarthroplasty (elderly, low-demand) or total hip arthroplasty (active elderly, pre-existing arthritis)
- Intertrochanteric: sliding hip screw (stable pattern) or cephalomedullary nail (unstable/reverse obliquity pattern)
- Subtrochanteric: cephalomedullary nail (long)

**Nonoperative Management (rare):**
- Reserved for patients with prohibitive surgical risk (terminal illness, bedbound at baseline, unable to tolerate any anesthesia)
- Comfort care pathway with pain management, DVT prophylaxis, early mobility as tolerated
- High mortality: 30-day mortality 17-25% without surgery

**Transfer:**
- Transfer to facility with orthopedic surgery and hip fracture surgical capability if not available locally
- Administer FICB, systemic analgesia, and initiate DVT prophylaxis before transfer
- Immobilize with pillow between legs; do not apply Buck traction for transport

guidance.title: Falls
guidance.summary:
Falls can be dangerous at any age. Babies and young children can get hurt falling off furniture or down the stairs. Older children may fall off playground equipment. For older adults, falls can be especially serious. They are at higher risk of falling. They are also more likely to fracture (break) a bone when they fall, especially if they have osteoporosis . A broken bone, especially when it is in a hip , may even lead to disability and a loss of independence for older adults. 

 Some common causes of falls include: 
 Balance problems 
 Some medicines, which can make you feel dizzy, confused, or slow 
 Vision problems 
 Alcohol, which can affect your balance and reflexes 
 Muscle weakness, especially in your legs, which can make it harder for you to get up from a chair or keep your balance when walking on an uneven surface. 
 Certain illnesses, such as low blood pressure , diabetes , and neuropathy 
 Slow reflexes, which make it hard to keep your balance or move out of the way of a hazard 
 Tripping or slipping due to loss of footing or traction 
 

 At any age, people can make changes to lower their risk of falling. It important to take care of your health, including getting regular eye exams . Regular exercise may lower your risk of falls by strengthening your muscles, improving your balance, and keeping your bones strong. And you can look for ways to make your house safer. For example, you can get rid of tripping hazards and make sure that you have rails on the stairs and in the bath. To reduce the chances of breaking a bone if you do fall, make sure that you get enough calcium and vitamin D . 

 NIH: National Institute on Aging

guidance.title: Hip Fracture
guidance.summary:
1. **Discharging an elderly fall patient with hip pain and negative X-rays without MRI.** Hip fracture is the number one missed fracture in older adults. Occult fractures occur in 2-10% of patients with negative radiographs. Any elderly patient unable to bear weight after a fall with groin or hip pain requires MRI (or CT if MRI is unavailable) before discharge.

2. **Failing to obtain a cross-table lateral hip radiograph.** An AP pelvis alone misses a significant proportion of femoral neck fractures. The lateral view reveals displacement and angulation not visible on AP. Both views are the minimum standard.

3. **Underestimating blood loss in intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric fractures.** These extracapsular fractures can bleed 500-1500 mL into the thigh with no visible external hemorrhage. Hemoglobin on arrival may be falsely normal due to hemoconcentration. Repeat hemoglobin at 6-8 hours. Type and screen all hip fracture patients on arrival.

4. **Inadequate pain management with systemic opioids alone.** IV opioid monotherapy in elderly hip fracture patients causes sedation, respiratory depression, constipation, and delirium while providing suboptimal analgesia. Fascia iliaca block is first-line — it reduces opioid requirements by 40-60% and decreases delirium incidence. Perform the block in the ED, do not defer to anesthesia.

5. **Delaying orthopedic consultation and surgical scheduling.** Surgery within 24-48 hours is the single most impactful modifiable factor for mortality reduction. Emergency physicians should notify orthopedics at the time of diagnosis and initiate preoperative workup simultaneously, not sequentially.

guidance.title: Femur Fracture
guidance.summary:
**Pre-operative management:**
- Traction splint for shaft fractures (reduces fracture, controls bleeding)
- Femoral nerve block for analgesia (see dosing above)
- DVT prophylaxis: enoxaparin 40 mg SQ daily or mechanical compression (initiate pre-operatively per institutional protocol)
- NPO for surgical planning

**Surgical fixation — timing matters:**
- **Elderly hip fractures:** Surgery within 24-48 hours reduces mortality, delirium, pneumonia, pressure ulcers (AAOS guideline). Every 24-hour delay increases 30-day mortality by 5%.
- **Young displaced femoral neck fractures:** Emergent reduction and fixation within 6-12 hours to minimize AVN risk
- **Shaft fractures in polytrauma:** "Damage control orthopedics" — temporary external fixation acutely, definitive intramedullary nailing at 24-72 hours when physiologically stable
- **Isolated shaft fractures:** Intramedullary nailing within 24 hours

**Surgical options:**
- **Femoral neck (young):** Closed reduction + percutaneous cannulated screws (Garden I-II); open reduction + internal fixation or hip arthroplasty (Garden III-IV)
- **Femoral neck (elderly displaced):** Hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty
- **Intertrochanteric:** Dynamic hip screw (DHS) or cephalomedullary nail (trochanteric fixation nail)
- **Subtrochanteric:** Cephalomedullary nail (long)

guidance.summary:
### Life-Threatening
- **Ruptured AAA** (`ruptured-aaa`): age > 60, sudden onset back/abdominal/flank pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass. Often misdiagnosed as renal colic. Classic triad (pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass) present in < 50%.

guidance.title: Femur Fracture
guidance.summary:
**Mechanism:**
- **Shaft fractures:** High-energy trauma (MVC, motorcycle, fall from height) in young adults; low-energy falls in elderly with osteoporosis
- **Neck/intertrochanteric fractures:** Fall in elderly (> 90% are age > 65); high-energy in young patients
- **Pathologic fractures:** Metastatic disease, osteoporosis — minimal or no trauma

**Classification:**
- **Femoral neck (intracapsular):** Garden I-IV. Displaced fractures (Garden III-IV) at risk for AVN due to disruption of circumflex femoral artery blood supply.
- **Intertrochanteric (extracapsular):** Stable vs. unstable patterns. Lower AVN risk.
- **Subtrochanteric:** High biomechanical stress area; often comminuted. Significant blood loss.
- **Shaft (diaphyseal):** AO/OTA classification. Associated with 1-1.5 L blood loss per fracture.

**Presentation:**
- Severe pain in thigh or hip, inability to bear weight
- Shortened, externally rotated leg (displaced hip fracture)
- Thigh swelling, deformity (shaft fracture)
- Hemodynamic instability (shaft fractures can lose 1-1.5 L per fracture; bilateral = massive hemorrhage)
- Open fracture: bone protruding through skin, soft tissue wound

**Associated injuries (high-energy mechanism):**
- Ipsilateral knee ligament injury (10-15%)
- Femoral neck fracture with shaft fracture (2-6% — easily missed)
- Hip dislocation
- Pelvic fracture
- Vascular injury (femoral artery, popliteal with distal fractures)
- Fat embolism syndrome (12-48 hours post-injury)

Hip replacement is surgery for people with severe hip damage. The most common cause of damage is osteoarthritis . Osteoarthritis causes pain, swelling, and reduced motion in your joints. It can interfere with your daily activities. If other treatments such as physical therapy, pain medicines, and exercise haven't helped, hip replacement surgery might be an option for you. 

 During a hip replacement operation, the surgeon removes damaged cartilage and bone from your hip joint and replaces them with new, man-made parts. 

 A hip replacement can: 
 Relieve pain 
 Help your hip joint work better 
 Improve walking and other movements 
 

 The most common problem after surgery is hip dislocation. Because a man-made hip is smaller than the original joint, the ball can come out of its socket. The surgery can also cause blood clots and infections. With a hip replacement, you might need to avoid certain activities, such as jogging and high-impact sports. 


 NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin

It can interfere with your daily activities. If other treatments such as physical therapy, pain medicines, and exercise haven't helped, hip replacement surgery might be an option for you. 

 During a hip replacement operation, the surgeon removes damaged cartilage and bone from your hip joint and replaces them with new, man-made parts. 

 A hip replacement can: 
 Relieve pain 
 Help your hip joint work better 
 Improve walking and other movements 
 

 The most common problem after surgery is hip dislocation. Because a man-made hip is smaller than the original joint, the ball can come out of its socket. The surgery can also cause blood clots and infections. With a hip replacement, you might need to avoid certain activities, such as jogging and high-impact sports.

1. **Delaying antibiotics.** Antibiotic administration within 1 hour of injury is the single most important intervention to prevent infection. Do not wait for orthopedic consultation, imaging, or OR availability. Time to antibiotics is more impactful than time to OR debridement.

2. **Missing a small open fracture wound.** A 3mm puncture wound near a tibial fracture is an open fracture. Any wound near a fracture is open until proven otherwise. Examine the entire circumference of the limb. Document wounds on the opposite side of the limb from the fracture (inside-out mechanism).

3. **Repeatedly exposing the wound for serial exams.** Photograph the wound once and cover it. Each exposure introduces additional contamination. Serial wound inspections by multiple providers worsen outcomes.

4. **Omitting gram-negative coverage for Gustilo Type III.** Type III open fractures have high rates of gram-negative infection. Cefazolin alone is insufficient — add gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV.

5. **Using fluoroquinolones for gram-negative coverage.** Ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin have been associated with higher infection rates and impaired fracture healing in open fractures compared to aminoglycosides. Gentamicin is the preferred agent.

6. **Forgetting tetanus prophylaxis.** Open fractures are tetanus-prone wounds. Check vaccination status and administer Tdap +/- TIG. This is missed frequently in the rush of trauma resuscitation.

7. **Failing to assess for compartment syndrome.** High-energy open fractures (especially tibial) are at risk for concurrent compartment syndrome. An open fracture does not decompress the compartment — fascial compartments may still be intact with elevated pressures.

chunk.text:
Falls can be dangerous at any age. Babies and young children can get hurt falling off furniture or down the stairs. Older children may fall off playground equipment. For older adults, falls can be especially serious. They are at higher risk of falling. They are also more likely to fracture (break) a bone when they fall, especially if they have osteoporosis . A broken bone, especially when it is in a hip , may even lead to disability and a loss of independence for older adults. 

 Some common causes of falls include: 
 Balance problems 
 Some medicines, which can make you feel dizzy, confused, or slow 
 Vision problems 
 Alcohol, which can affect your balance and reflexes 
 Muscle weakness, especially in your legs, which can make it harder for you to get up from a chair or keep your balance when walking on an uneven surface. 
 Certain illnesses, such as low blood pressure , diabetes , and neuropathy 
 Slow reflexes, which make it hard to keep your balance or move out of the way of a hazard 
 Tripping or slipping due to loss of footing or traction 
 

 At any age, people can make changes to lower their risk of falling. It important to take care of your health, including getting regular eye exams . Regular exercise may lower your risk of falls by strengthening your muscles, improving your balance, and keeping your bones strong. And you can look for ways to make your house safer. For example, you can get rid of tripping hazards and make sure that you have rails on the stairs and in the bath. To reduce the chances of breaking a bone if you do fall, make sure that you get enough calcium and vitamin D . 

 NIH: National Institute on Aging

 The goals for treating osteoporosis are to slow or stop bone loss and to prevent fractures. Your provider may recommend: 
 
 A healthy, balanced diet that includes enough calcium, vitamin D, and protein 
 Lifestyle changes such as quitting smoking and limiting alcohol 
 Regular physical activity including weight-bearing exercise (like walking), strength training, and balance exercises 
 Fall prevention to help prevent fractures 
 Medicines, such as:
 
 Medicines that slow down bone loss

 Twisting your spine, like swinging a golf club 
 Bending forward from the waist, like sit ups and toe touches
